The pilot's failure to obtain a proper touchdown point while landing with a gusting tailwind.
The local air traffic controller's failure to follow published procedures and directives, resulting in a landing airplane coming in close proximity to runway workers.
The pilot's loss of situational awareness while maneuvering in adverse weather conditions, resulting in spatial disorientation.

The tower controller's failure to ensure the runway was clear before allowing Skywest 69R to land.  Factors contributing to the incident were the Malibu pilot's and tower controller's unfamiliarity with the airport layout.

The pilot's failure to extend the landing gear before touchdown. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's failure to perform the appropriate checklist due to distractions posed by another airplane inbound to the same airport and a cluttered radio frequency.
The pilot's loss of directional control while landing in gusting crosswind conditions, which exceeded the airplane's maximum demonstrated crosswind velocity.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.
The separation of the control grip which resulted in the pilot’s inability to maintain directional control during takeoff, and collision with terrain.
The pilot's intentional low-altitude operation, which resulted in his failure to maintain clearance from unmarked utility wires.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's disorientation as a result of dust which reduced visibility.
The failure of the left main landing gear leg due to fatigue. Contributing to the incident was maintenance personnel's failure to completely remove all corrosion before repainting the gear leg.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing roll-out. Contributing to the accident was the worn left main landing gear brake.
The pilot's loss of directional control during landing, resulting in a runway excursion.
The flight instructor's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, resulting in an impact with an unknown object during aborted landing and consequent ground impact.
The pilot’s failure to maintain adequate airspeed during landing, which led to the airplane exceeding its critical angle-of-attack and experiencing an aerodynamic stall.

The pilot’s failure to maintain proper airspeed and his exceedance of the airplane’s critical angle of attack during initial climb after takeoff, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall and impact with the ground.
A stuck aileron due to a battery that had become jammed in the aileron bell crank.
The partial loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined based on available evidence.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the takeoff roll.
An in-flight collision with a bird.
the A330 flightcrew's failure to maintain a safe clearance between his wing and the tail of the DHC-8-400 that was stopped on the lead in line of the gate.

the nose landing gear alternate release handle was not pulled with sufficient enough force or distance to release the uplocks and allow extension of the nose landing gear.

The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, which resulted in a ground loop.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing, which resulted in runway excursion and collision with terrain.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control of the airplane during the takeoff roll.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the takeoff roll on a rough turf runway.
Overload failure of the left main landing gear during landing, which resulted in a loss of directional control.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control of the tailwheel-equipped airplane, which resulted in a ground-loop.

A total loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined because a postaccident examination of the engine and fuel system found no mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
The pilot’s loss of directional control during landing which led to a ground-loop.
A fatigue failure of a copper oil line, which resulted in a partial loss of engine power due to oil starvation.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.

The pilot's attempt to land in strong crosswind conditions, resulting in his on-ground loss of control. Contributing to the accident was the crosswind that exceeded the crosswind limits of the airplane.
The pilot's inability to maintain control during landing due to seized main landing gear wheels, which caused the airplane to nose over.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll in gusting wind.
Impact with terrain for reasons that could not be determined based on the available information.
The pilot's failure to maintain adequate airspeed that resulted in a stall/mush. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's failure to maintain an adequate spacing from the aircraft ahead of him.
A total loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.

The installation of an unapproved rudder control cable, which resulted in a fatigue failure and subsequent loss of rudder control during cruise flight. Contributing to the accident was the mechanic’s inadequate inspection of the rudder control system.
The pilot’s failure to maintain direction control of the airplane during the landing roll.
The pilot's inadvertent contact with the propeller while hand propping the engine, which resulted in a fatal injury.

The pilot's improper in-flight fuel management and reliance on a faulty fuel gauge, which resulted in fuel starvation during approach for landing, and his failure to follow the emergency checklist after losing engine power.

The failure of the pilot of the other airplane to maintain adequate clearance while performing an unexpected and unannounced abrupt maneuver, resulting in a midair collision between the two airplanes.

The total loss of engine power for undetermined reasons during low altitude cruise flight, which resulted in a water ditching. Contributing to the severity of the accident was the pilot’s failure to extend the flaps during the ditching, which increased the impact forces to the occupants.

The pilot’s inadequate visual lookout while departing from a multiple-use waterway, which resulted in a collision with a drifting boat. Contributing to the accident were the lack of visual conspicuity of the boat and the limited amount of time the boat operator had to maneuver the boat once he heard
The pilot's decision to initiate a go-around after a bounced landing at an airport where go-arounds were not advised and his failure to maintain adequate airspeed during the go-around.

The pilot’s inability to maintain aircraft control due to a partial loss of engine power and an encounter with downdrafts and gusting crosswinds while on final approach to the runway. Maintenance personnel’s application of insufficient torque to the engine cylinder through bolts during replacement of the No. 1 cylinder, which resulted in the displacement of the No. 2 main bearing, the bearing shifting, and a catastrophic engine failure.
An encounter with wind gusts, which resulted in a loss of control and a collapse of the nose landing gear.

An autopilot deviation during climb for undetermined reasons, which resulted in an in-flight upset and loss of airplane control. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s failure to adequately monitor flight systems due to a distraction.
The pilot’s improper maintenance of the ignition system, which led to an ignition system failure and a loss of engine power.

The pilot's failure to use carburetor heat while operating at low power settings in conditions conducive to the development of carburetor ice, and the subsequent total loss of engine power due to carburetor icing.
The biplane pilot’s inadequate visual lookout while taxing, which resulted in a ground collision.

The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during takeoff and subsequent rejected takeoff, which resulted in a runway excursion. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s failure to verify rudder trim setting prior to takeoff.
The pilot’s delayed decision to perform a go-around after an unstabilized approach, which resulted in a loss of control, runway overrun, and impact with terrain.
The loss of directional control for undetermined reasons. Contributing was the overstress fracture of the nose gear upper trunnion brace attach point.
